documents.title: NHMRC clinical practice guidelines for depression

chunks.content: Introduction Depression and anxiety are prevalent psychiatric disorders that are associated with high rates of disability and suicide, which have been increasingly becoming a major challenge to global public health [ – ]. According to the 2021 Global Burden of Disease (GBD) Study [ , ], approximately 341 million people worldwide suffer from depression, and about 53.9 million are troubled by anxiety disorders. Despite the availability of evidence-based prevention and treatment interventions, these psychiatric disorder continue to impose great mental stress and heavy economic burdens to patients, and also give rise to numerous social problems. It is noteworthy that comorbidity of anxiety and depression reached as high as 50% to 60% [ ]. This comorbidity is associated with a substantially increased risk of suicidal ideation (SID) and suicide attempts, which provide substantial challenges for clinical diagnosis and treatment decisions [ – ]. Therefore, the precise discrimination of depression, anxiety and their comorbidities, along hierarchical management, has received increasing attention and become a research hotspot in the current field of mental health. Currently, the diagnosis of psychiatric disorders primarily relies on clinical interviews and clinician-administered scales. However, these methods are limited by subjective assessment, clinician-patient communication, and cultural influences, which may lead to diagnostic bias or misdiagnosis [ , ]. Given the substantial overlap in clinical symptoms and the potentially shared neurobiological mechanisms among anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity, traditional symptom-based diagnostic approaches often lack sufficient specificity for differential identification [ – ]. However, studies in the past have shown depression or anxiety as distinct disorders, whereas relatively few have specifically focused on the differential diagnosis for comorbid of anxiety and depression [ , ]. In addition, some studies rely on complex or less accessible features, and many lack sufficient interpretability or clinically oriented evaluation, which may limit their application in routine clinical practice. Therefore, there is an urgent requirement to develop cost-effective and accurate auxiliary diagnostic tools to improve the identification and risk stratification of anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity. Heart rate variability (HRV) is a non-invasive indicator used to evaluate autonomic nervous system (ANS) function, which objectively reflects the dynamic balance between sympathetic and parasympathetic activity [ , ]. Previous studies have consistently demonstrated that patients with depression or anxiety exhibit significantly lower HRV, which reflect diminished ability to regulate emotions and physiological responses to stress [ , ]. These findings indicated that HRV is expected to become an important potential biomarker for clinical diagnosis, disease stratification and prognosis assessment of psychiatric disorders [ – ]. With the rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) technology and data sciences, machine learning (ML) has become widely used in public health and medical research fields [ – ]. In recent years, ML-based models have demonstrated outstanding performance in the early diagnosis and screening of psychiatric disorders such as depression or anxiety, particularly in evaluating treatment response and prognosis [ , ]. Thus, we hypothesize that incorporating HRV features and clinical indicators may yield promising efficiency in distinguishing early-stage depression, anxiety, and psychiatric comorbidities. In this study, we aimed to develop and validate an interpretable, multi-task ML prediction model for the early and accurate discrimination of depression alone, anxiety alone, and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. By analyzing the relationship between HRV feature and psychiatric symptoms, we explored how these variables might affect psychiatric disorders. The SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) method was used to visualize feature contributions and enhance the interpretability of models, which is helpful for providing clinical decision-making for clinicians. Methods Study design The study design adheres to the Transparent Reporting of a multivariable prediction model for Individual Prognosis or Diagnosis (TRIPOD) statement. The overall workflow of this study is illustrated in Fig. , which comprises three main components: data acquisition, feature extraction, model construction and validation. Study population This retrospective study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University (KY2024507), with the requirement for informed consent waived. All patient-related information was anonymous and de-identified. The study protocol was conducted in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki. Data of patients who underwent psychological assessment between March 2024 and April 2025, were obtained from the Department of Psychiatry, the Affiliated Hospital of Southwest Medical University. The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) aged ≥ 14 years; (ii) cognitive ability to understand and complete assessments of the depression and anxiety scale, including HRV measurements; (iii) no gender restrictions; (iv) no severe major cardiovascular diseases, liver or kidney dysfunction. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) patients with missing HRV data; (ii) presence of other psychiatric disorders, such as bipolar disorder or personality disorders; (iii) patients with severe cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart failure or coronary artery disease), chronic liver or kidney disease, or other diseases potentially affecting HRV (e.g., acute infection or fever); and

The inclusion criteria were as follows: (i) aged ≥ 14 years; (ii) cognitive ability to understand and complete assessments of the depression and anxiety scale, including HRV measurements; (iii) no gender restrictions; (iv) no severe major cardiovascular diseases, liver or kidney dysfunction. The exclusion criteria were as follows: (i) patients with missing HRV data; (ii) presence of other psychiatric disorders, such as bipolar disorder or personality disorders; (iii) patients with severe cardiovascular disease (e.g., heart failure or coronary artery disease), chronic liver or kidney disease, or other diseases potentially affecting HRV (e.g., acute infection or fever); and (iv) pregnant or breastfeeding women. In this study, a total of 546 patients were included, 114 patients with anxiety, 100 patients with depression, and 332 patients with comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The task of discriminating psychiatric comorbidities was recast into two binary classification events: (i) anxiety versus (vs.) comorbidity of anxiety and depression, and (ii) depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression. According to different tasks, patients were respectively divided into training and validation sets at an approximately 7:3 ratio. Stratified random sampling was employed to ensure that the proportion of positive and negative samples was consistent in the two sets. The flowchart of the study population in Fig. . Clinical assessment and HRV measurement The clinical diagnosis and HRV measurements of patients in the study were rigorously performed by trained psychiatrists in accordance with standardized procedures to ensure consistency and accuracy. According to patient self-reports and clinical interviews, we employed clinician-administered scales to assess various dimensions of psychiatric symptoms, including mood, somatic discomfort, and cognitive function. Outcome measures for diagnosing anxiety, depression and comorbidities assessed included the 24-item Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HAMD-24) [ , ] and the 14-item Hamilton Anxiety Scale (HAMA-14) [ , ]. The HAMD-24 was used to evaluate the level of depressive symptoms. The total score of HAMD Scale < 8 is no depression, 8–19 is mild depression, 20–34 is moderate depression, and ≥ 35 is severe depression. The HAMA-14 was used to evaluate the severity of anxious symptoms. The total score of HAMA Scale < 7 is no anxiety, 7–13 is possible anxiety, 14–20 is moderate anxiety, and ≥ 21 is severe anxiety. To reduce potential misclassification due to mild symptom presentation or subjective bias, the comorbidity of anxiety and depression was included when participants met at least moderate symptom severity based on Hamilton scale cutoffs (HAMD ≥ 20 and HAMA ≥ 14). The HRV measurements were conducted using a HRV analyzer system (VitalScan, Credit Pharmaceutical Co., Ltd., Sichuan, China; https://www.creditpharma.com/ ). Participants were instructed to get sufficient sleep and avoid excessive drinking, smoking, taking caffeine or drugs, and strenuous exercise prior to testing. The HRV measurement environment was maintained with quiet, bright, and soft lighting, block out external noise, and keep a suitable room temperature (20–25℃) to reduce external interference. The electrodes were connected to the three-lead electrocardiogram signal at the standard position, and the basic subject’s information is entered on the operation interface. Subsequently, electrocardiogram (ECG) signals were continuously collected within 5 min for HRV analysis. Upon completion, the system automatically generated and stored an individualized HRV report for each participant. Data collection and preprocessing A total of 17 features were screened out from the case reports, including 2 demographic features (gender, age), 2 clinical features (BMI, heart rate), and 13 HRV features. The HRV features include time-domain features, frequency-domain features, and nonlinear features, which are details in Table . After splitting the training and the validation set, the synthetic minority over-sampling algorithm (SMOTE) was used to balance the positive and negative samples in the training set [ ]. Then, we utilized the Yeo-Johnson power transformation for data normalization. The transformation parameters were fitted in the training set and subsequently applied to the validation set to ensure the model consistency and avoid data leakage [ ]. To prevent over-fitting and increased the generalization ability of the model, the recursive feature elimination (RFE) algorithm with 10-fold cross-validation was used for feature selection [ ]. This method iteratively eliminates features in a backward manner, ranking feature importance and retaining the subset with the strongest discriminative ability [ ]. Through 10-fold cross-validation, the number of retained features (k) is determined in the training set, and then we selected the top k ranked important features to construct models for each task. Model development and validation Six machine-learning algorithms, including logistic regression (LR), support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), k-nearest neighbors (KNN), and Naïve Bayes (NB) were adopted to develop prediction models for discriminating psychiatric comorbidities, respectively (Supplementary Appendix S1).Then, a comparison of these models was also performed in both the training and validation set. To ensure the stability and generalization ability of the models, a grid search combined with 10-fold cross validation was used to determine the best hyperparameters [ , ] (Supplementary Appendix , Table a and b). The discrimination ability of these models was evaluated using multiple metrics, including the area of receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC), accuracy (ACC), sensitivity (SEN), specificity (SPE), positive predictive value (PPV), negative predictive value (NPV), F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC). The 1,000-bootstrap resamples strategy was used for internal validation, and the 95% confidence intervals (CIs) was calculated. The model calibration was evaluated using the Calibration curves accompanied by the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test (HL test). Decision curve analysis (DCA) was performed to quantify the net clinical benefit across a range of threshold probabilities, thereby evaluating the potential clinical utility of the predictive models. Model interpretability with Shapley Additive explanation (SHAP) In this study, we utilized SHAP method to quantify the contribution and influence of each feature toward the overall prediction result, thereby providing a visual interpretation for the machine-learning model with the best predictive performance to facilitate clinical decision-making [ , ]. The SHAP value indicates that each feature has a positive or negative impact on the probability of the outcome prediction. Besides, we generated force plots to visualize the key features that affect the decision-making process of the best model. Statistical analysis All statistical analysis were performed using R software (version 4.3.0) and Python (version 3.11.7). Continuous variables were expressed as medians, first (Q1) and third (Q3) quartiles, and ranges, and categorical variables were expressed in terms of frequencies and percentages (%). Comparisons between groups were calculated using the Chi-square or the Fisher’s exact test for categorical variables, and the Kruskal-Wallis rank-sum test for continuous variables. All P were two-tailed, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Baseline characteristics A total of 546 patients, 114 patients in anxiety group(20.88%), 100 patients in depression group (18.32%), and 332 patients in comorbidity of anxiety and depression (60.81%), were included in this study. The baseline characteristics of all patients are shown in Table . The significant group differences were observed in age, gender, heart rate, pNN50, RMSSD, SDSD, VLF, HF, SD1, and SD1/SD2 ( P < 0.05), whereas no significant differences were found for BMI, SDNN, SDNN5, SD2, LF, TP and LF/HF ( P > 0.05). Among the three groups, the proportion of female patients in the comorbidity group (81.63%) was higher than in the anxiety group (70.18%) and the depression group (72.00%). Variable selection We used the RFE algorithm with 10-fold cross-validation to rank the importance of features in the training set for different tasks, and the scoring results for each variable were displayed in a bar plot. For the anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression task, the top 11 feature were selected as independent factors for modelling, such as gender, age, HF, VLF, LF/HF, BMI, heart rate, SDNN5, LF, pNN50, and SD1/SD2 (Supplementary Fig. a). Similarly, for the depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, we ultimately selected the top 11 feature as prediction factors for modelling, including LF, gender, SD2, VLF, SDNN, LF/HF, heart rate, TP, HF, SD1/SD2, and BMI (Supplementary Fig. b). Development and validation of prediction models The performance of six machine-learning models for discriminating psychiatric comorbidities was comprehensively evaluated using AUC, ACC, SEN, SPE, PPV, NPV, F1-score, and MCC. Across two binary classification tasks in this study, the XGBoost model demonstrated superior performance compared with the other five machine-learning models as shown in Fig. . For the task of discriminating the anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, the XGBoost model yielded the AUC of 0.8341 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.761–0.907), F1-score of 0.764 and accuracy of 0.7650 (95% CI:0.682–0.848) in the validation set. (Fig. A and B; Table ). For the task of discriminating the depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, the XGBoost model achieved the AUC of 0.8458 (95% CI:0.775–0.917) F1-score of 0.784 and accuracy of 0.7850 (95% CI:0.704–0.866) in the validation set. (Fig. C and D; Table ). To assess the agreement between the predicted and observed outcomes, we constructed calibration curves (1000 bootstrap resamples) for the XGBoost models across two classification tasks. The calibration plots for all classification tasks remained ideal, indicating good stability and clinical utility of the XGBoost model in both the training and validation sets (Fig. ). In addition, we performed decision curve analysis (DCA) to evaluate the potential clinical utility of the models by quantifying the net benefit across a broad range of threshold probabilities. The x-axis represents the threshold probability (ranging from 0 to 1), while the y-axis represents the net clinical benefit at each threshold (Fig. ). Across all classification tasks, the XGBoost model consistently achieved a higher net benefit over a wide range of thresholds, indicating the model’s practical utility in clinical diagnosis and decision-making. Model interpretation and visualisation using the SHAP method In this study, the SHAP method was used to visually interpret the best model (XGBoost). We employed the SHAP values to quantitatively illustrate how each feature affects the final prediction outcomes under different feature combinations. The bar chart shows that the higher SHAP value of feature, where a larger value has a greater influence the model’s prediction. The beeswarm plot SHAP values are colour-coded to reveal the relationship between each features and the prediction outcomes, where blue represents lower feature values and red represents higher feature values. The SHAP force plots provide a visual representation of how each feature influences the final prediction f (x) starting from the model’s baseline prediction value (baseline). For the classification of anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, Fig. A and B shows that gender and age were the most important features that have impact on the prediction outcomes, followed by VLF, pNN50, LF/HF, HF, BMI, SD1/SD2, LF, heart rate, and SDNN5. Among all HRV features, VLF has the highest SHAP influence, indicating that higher VLF levels have a stronger impact on the model’s predictions. Figure C and D correspond to the same individual (comorbidity of anxiety and depression). The HF, pNN50, BMI, SD1/SD2, VLF, and gender are the main risk-increasing indicators for comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Meanwhile, LF and LF/HF are the risk-reducing indicators for this comorbidity, though their contributions are relatively small. The final prediction value is 0.702 (> 0.5), which indicates that this patient has a relatively high risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression. For the classification of depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, Fig. A and B shows that LF and gender were the most important features that have impact on the prediction outcomes, followed by VLF, SD1/SD2, heart rate, HF, BMI, TP, LF/HF, SDNN, and SD2. Among all HRV features, LF has the highest SHAP influence, indicating that higher LF levels have a stronger impact on the model’s predictions. Figure C and D correspond to the another individual (depression). The SD2, BMI, and LF are main risk-increasing factors for comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Meanwhile, gender, SD1/SD2, and heart rate are a risk-reducing factor for this comorbidity, though their contributions are relatively small. The final prediction value reaches 0.318 (< 0.5), which indicates that this patient has a relatively low risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression. Discussion To our knowledge, machine learning has significant advantages for risk prediction and pattern recognition in complex disorders. This study is the first to develop and evaluate multi-task prediction models to discriminate psychiatric comorbidity status using the HRV features. By comparing six ML algorithms, we identified the the best-performing ML algorithm for predicting risk associated with psychiatric disorders. Across two binary classification tasks, our models demonstrated consistently excellent performance in the validation set, with AUCs (95% CIs) of 0.8341 (95% CI:0.761–0.907) for anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, 0.8458 (95% CI:0.775–0.917) for depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The final model incorporated basic clinical data and HRV features to ensure simplicity, user-friendliness, and potential clinical utility, and also demonstrated strong generalization ability and stability. To improve interpretability and clinical application of models, we employed SHAP to visualized global and local model explanations, which is helpful for providing timely appropriate intervention for patients with psychiatric disorders. Depression, anxiety, and their comorbidity are multifactorial and potentially life-threatening psychiatric disorders, they have similar clinical symptoms and are difficult to strictly discriminate. Our findings showed that anxiety, depression, and comorbidities of anxiety and depression are all significantly associated with reduced HRV features. Depression, anxiety, and their comorbidity are multifactorial and potentially life-threatening psychiatric disorders, they have similar clinical symptoms and are difficult to strictly discriminate. Our findings showed that anxiety, depression, and comorbidities of anxiety and depression are all significantly associated with reduced HRV features. The demographic features (gender, age) may be associated with the risk of comorbidity of anxiety and depression, potentially linked to differences in hormonal regulation, cognitive development, and emotional processing mechanisms [ , ]. Specifically, comorbid patients exhibit higher resting heart rates and lower HRV characteristic variables (such as RMSSD, SDSD, SD1, SD1/SD2, VLF and HF), which indicated they were significantly autonomic dysregulation compared to patients with depression or anxiety alone. These findings are consistent with previous studies [ – ], which characterized by dual abnormalities of increased sympathetic activity and vagal inhibition, which is specifically characterized by a dual disturbance pattern involving abnormally heightened sympathetic nerve activity and impaired vagal regulatory function. This imbalance affects cardiac autonomic regulation and cause physiological dysfunction across multiple systems through the neuro-humoral regulatory pathway, including the endocrine and digestive systems [ – ]. To further explore the decision-making logic driving model prediction, SHAP analysis were applied to hierarchically interpret the optimal model by providing the feature contributions from the population to the individual level. Compared with traditional feature ranking methods, SHAP can reveal how the model integrates feature information at different levels, thereby significantly enhancing model transparency and clinical interpretability [ ]. For the classification task of anxiety vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, SHAP visualizations indicated that VLF, pNN50, LF/HF, and HF were key contributors to the model’s predictions. The decreased VLF has been typically associated with increased cardiovascular disease risk, impaired autonomic nerve function and chronic stress, which may be the reason for more severe autonomic dysfunction observed in comorbid patients [ , ]. The pNN50 mainly reflects the regulatory ability of the parasympathetic nerve relative to heart rate [ ]. The decreased HF leads to vagal dysfunction, exacerbate emotional instability and abnormal stress responses, which may indicate that anxious patients with decreased HF have a potential risk of deteriorating into complex comorbid patients [ ]. Our findings reveal that the elevated LF/HF ratio was positively correlated with comorbidity risk [ ], which may reflect a significant alteration in the autonomic nerve regulation pattern of comorbid patients compared to anxiety patients alone [ ]. For the classification task of depression vs. comorbidity of anxiety and depression, SHAP visualizations indicated that LF, VLF, SD1/SD2, heart rate, and HF emerged as the most influential features. The LF primarily reflects the integrated sympathetic-vagal regulatory activity under pressure reflex modulation, the abnormal variation of LF value indicate that comorbid patients may exhibit autonomic dysfunction [ ]. The SD1/SD2 ratio reflects the complexity of autonomic nerve regulation and dynamic adaptability. The decreased SD1/SD2 may reduce the coordinated regulatory ability of the autonomic nervous system, which is consistent with the occurrence of more severe autonomic dysfunction in patients with comorbid anxiety and depression [ ]. The SHAP contributions of LF, VLF, and HF exhibit pronounced nonlinearity across individuals, indicating that they possess heterogeneity rather than simple unidirectional effects when discriminating comorbid patients and depression alone. Our findings reveal that the VLF was correlated with comorbid patients, which indicated that comorbid patients exhibit more complex ANS dysregulation compared to depression or anxiety alone. Notably, VLF proved significant across two classification tasks, highlighting the cross-task value of the autonomic nerve function regulatory mechanisms for identifying complex psychiatric symptom. This finding indicates that VLF may serve as a potential key HRV indicator for identifying comorbidity of anxiety and depression, though the mechanism requires further validation in prospective studies. From a clinical perspective, our findings have potential significant implications for improving symptom management and intervention strategies. HRV, as a non-invasive, accessible, and cost-effective physiological indicator, can rapidly reflect ANS function, which has been widely proved to be closely associated with anxiety, depression, and their comorbidity [ , ]. Therefore, the ML-based models incorporating HRV features can provide clinicians with an objective auxiliary assessment tool for early identification of high-risk individuals. This approach may be particularly valuable in primary care settings or regions with limited healthcare resources, where it can serve as a screening tool to improve the efficiency of identifying suspected patients. Additionally, for patients who have already been diagnosed with anxiety or depression, regular monitoring of HRV indicators can help track disease progression, promptly identify high-risk individuals evolving to comorbidities, and thereby provide targeted interventions strategies. However, there were several limitations in our study. Firstly, this retrospective single-center study has a relatively limited-size sample and predominantly adolescent participants (median age 16 years), which may introduce potential selection bias and constrains generalisability to other populations. To address this, future multi-center studies will incorporate prospective data and expand the sample size of different age populations before actual clinical application. Secondly, our findings only included HRV and conventional clinical features, more clinical features such as clinical drug use, follow-up, genes, neuroimaging and inflammatory markers were not included in this study. Thirdly, this study only discriminate psychiatric comorbidity and failed to involve the prediction of treatment responses, thereby preventing the model from accounting for regimen-specific effects. Finally, although HRV serves as a non-invasive indicator of autonomic activity, which represents only an indirect marker of the complex heart-brain interactions for emotional regulation and psychiatric symptoms. In future, we will employ a multimodal approach integrating HRV and electroencephalogram (EEG) signals to conduct comprehensive analyses of individual mental health states. Despite these limitations, our findings provide effective biomarkers for distinguishing individuals with psychiatric disorders, offering valuable support for advancing early prevention and timely intervention. Conclusions This study reveals the relationship between HRV features and different psychiatric symptoms, and explores HRV as a potential biomarker for the diagnosis of anxiety, depression, and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. we developed and validated an interpretable multi-task ML prediction model using HRV for the early and accurate discrimination of depression alone, anxiety alone and comorbidity of anxiety and depression. The superior performance highlighted the potential to aid clinical decision-making for the individualized treatment.
